case_title: Amar Singh v. The State (NCT of Delhi)
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute (alleged by the defence): the defence said the victim had been accused of murdering the father of accused Inderjeet Singh. The Court did not accept this.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.506; Arms Act s.25 and s.27 (charged against accused Inderjeet Singh); conviction under Arms Act s.27 for Inderjeet Singh
evidence_type: Eyewitness (sole remaining eyewitness, PW-1); medical (post-mortem and MLC); recovery (knife and hockey sticks)
confession: Disclosure statements led to recovery of the knife and hockey sticks; the Court did not rely on them as a confession
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and sentenced to life imprisonment with fine of Rs.5000 each; accused Inderjeet Singh also convicted under Arms Act s.27 and sentenced to one year rigorous imprisonment, concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld (judgment dated 09.05.2014)
neutral_facts: On the night of the incident, the victim was walking on foot with his two brothers toward a taxi stand in a market area at about 10 pm. Three men attacked the victim. Two were said to have struck him with hockey sticks and one with a knife. When the brothers tried to help, the attackers brandished their weapons and threatened to kill anyone who intervened. The victim collapsed and the attackers fled. After some time a police PCR van took the victim to a hospital, where he was declared brought dead. The post-mortem examination recorded around fifteen antemortem injuries caused by a sharp-edged weapon. The cause of death was given as shock from multiple antemortem injuries. Police recovered a knife and hockey sticks following statements by the accused persons. A medical clinic was located nearby. The hospital record initially listed the victim as unknown and recorded a head constable as the person who brought him in. The brothers said the attack lasted about five minutes. The sole eyewitness account came from one brother; the other brother and a third witness did not support the prosecution account at trial. The recovered knife had a broken, blunt tip. The doctor was not shown the knife to comment on whether it could cause the injuries.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock due to multiple antemortem injuries (about 15 injuries, including sharp-edged stab and incised wounds)
number_of_offences: 4 charged (IPC s.302, s.506, Arms Act s.25 and s.27; IPC s.34 is a common-intention provision); 0 finally upheld
motive: Not identified. Alleged by the defence: the victim's brothers had a motive to falsely implicate the accused because the victim was accused of murdering the father of accused Inderjeet Singh. The Court did not decide this.
key_evidence_accepted: The Court relied on the post-mortem finding of cause of death, but did not accept the eyewitness account or the MLC/recovery evidence as reliable
witness_credibility: PW-1 (sole eyewitness) found not wholly reliable and not shown to be present, given his unnatural conduct and the timing discrepancy. PW-11 and PW-5 turned hostile. The MLC (PW-17) entries cast doubt on the brothers' presence at the hospital.
trial_duration: offence: 03.08.1990; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 09.05.2014; Supreme Court: 12.10.2020
legal_representation: Accused: Dushyant Dave, Senior Advocate (with others listed). State: Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, ASG
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed with 27 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: Investigating officer did not show the recovered knife to the doctor; the MLC entries (name recorded as unknown, head constable as the person who brought the victim in, 'and brothers' added) were noted as irregular
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed (09.05.2014). Supreme Court: appeals allowed, accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: Concurrent findings of guilt rest on a reliable eyewitness; hostile witness evidence can be relied on in part; investigation lapses do not make the case doubtful where direct evidence is corroborated by medical evidence
defence_argument: The incident was inherently improbable; PW-1's conduct was unnatural, making his presence doubtful; the conviction rests on an uncorroborated sole eyewitness; the knife with a broken tip could not have caused the injuries; the victim's brothers had a motive to falsely implicate
legal_principle_applied: A sole eyewitness may be relied on if wholly reliable (Evidence Act s.134), but where doubts exist the Court insists on corroboration; unnatural conduct, medical discrepancy and investigative lapses can make conviction unsafe; benefit of doubt to accused
precedent_relied_upon: Kartarey v. State of U.P. (1976) 1 SCC 172; Ishwar Singh v. State of U.P. (1976) 4 SCC 355 (relied on). Also Sunil Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2003) 11 SCC 367 and Selvaraj v. State of Tamil Nadu (1976) 4 SCC 343 (referred to)
other_sentence_order: Release of appellants forthwith unless required in any other case
